assignmentHtml.task: Audit claims E1 and E2 about ESA's Juice mission. Starting point: https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Juice. Key questions: (1) Did Juice launch on 14 April 2023? (2) Is its planned Jupiter arrival in 2031 an accomplished observation that can be described in past tense as of Sept 2026? (3) Does Juice study ONLY Europa? Will it land on ice? (4) Is Juice the European name for NASA's Europa Clipper? Do Ganymede and Callisto need separate entries? Find ESA sources, mission pages, and any launch confirmation.
assignmentHtml.context: Mission: Juice (JUpiter ICy moons Explorer). Claims E1-E2: E1 says launched 14 Apr 2023, planned Jupiter arrival 2031 is accomplished/past-tense by cutoff Sept 2026. E2 says Juice studies only Europa, will land on ice, and is same spacecraft as NASA's Europa Clipper. These are claims to audit. Note: Juice and Europa Clipper are completely different missions.
assignmentHtml.expected_output: Verdict on each component of E1 and E2 with corrected text, dates, units, source URLs. Specifically: launch date, Jupiter arrival status as of Sept 2026, what planets/moons Juice targets, whether it lands, whether it's the same as Europa Clipper.

answerHtml:
AUDIT RESULTS FOR CLAIMS E1 AND E2 ABOUT ESA'S JUICE MISSION:

E1a — 'Launched 14 April 2023': TRUE. Juice launched on 14 April 2023 at 14:14 CEST from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, aboard an Ariane 5 rocket. Confirmed by ESA's main Juice page, ESA Cosmos mission calendar, NASA Astrobiology, and The Planetary Society.

E1b — 'Jupiter arrival in 2031 is accomplished/past-tense as of Sept 2026': FALSE. Juice's planned Jupiter arrival is 21 July 2031 (Jupiter Arrival and Orbit Insertion phase, per ESA Cosmos mission calendar). As of September 2026, Juice is still in interplanetary transit — specifically in its third Earth gravity assist (31 July – 29 October 2026). The arrival is a future event; describing it in past tense is incorrect and misleading. Correct phrasing: 'planned to arrive at Jupiter in July 2031.'

E2a — 'Juice studies ONLY Europa': FALSE. Juice studies Jupiter's three large ocean-bearing moons: Ganymede (primary target), Callisto, and Europa, plus Jupiter itself. The ESA main page states the mission will make 'detailed observations of the giant gas planet and its three large ocean-bearing moons – Ganymede, Callisto and Europa.' Ganymede is singled out as primary target and Juice will become the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than Earth's.

E2b — 'Will land on ice': FALSE. Juice is an orbital/flyby spacecraft with no landing capability. It will perform flybys of Europa (twice), Ganymede (12 times), and Callisto (12 times) during its Jupiter orbit phase, then enter orbit around Ganymede for at least nine months. ESA explicitly describes it as 'the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than our own.' Both Juice and Europa Clipper are slated for controlled impacts onto Ganymede at end-of-mission (disposal), but this is not a scientific landing.

E2c — 'Juice is the European name for NASA's Europa Clipper': FALSE. They are entirely separate missions. Juice is an ESA mission; Europa Clipper is a NASA mission (launched 14 October 2024 on Falcon Heavy). Juice focuses on Ganymede and the Jupiter system broadly; Europa Clipper dedicates ~50 flybys to Europa alone. ESA's own 'dream team' article states: 'Juice and Europa Clipper are independent missions with individual science goals.' They share no spacecraft hardware, designations, or identities.

Regarding Ganymede and Callisto separate entries: Yes, both require separate treatment from Europa. Juice's science targets are three distinct moons (Ganymede, Callisto, Europa), each requiring individual factual accuracy.

evidence.snippet: Launch: 14 April 2023. Arrival at Jupiter: July 2031. 'ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, Juice, will make detailed observations of the giant gas planet and its three large ocean-bearing moons – Ganymede, Callisto and Europa.'
evidence.supports: E1a launch date TRUE; E1b arrival in July 2031 is future tense; E2a Juice studies three moons, not only Europa.

evidence.snippet: 'JUICE was launch with an Arianne 5 on 14/04/2023, and following nominal injection it is planned to arrive to Jupiter on 21/07/2031.' Mission phases show Earth Gravity Assist sub-phase active 31/07/2026–29/10/2026. Jupiter Arrival phase listed 21/06/2031–22/07/2031.
evidence.supports: E1b: arrival is 21 July 2031, a future event; as of Sept 2026 Juice is mid-transit (Earth gravity assist), so describing arrival in past tense is false.

evidence.snippet: 'Europa Clipper will concentrate on Europa, while Juice will primarily focus on Ganymede while also providing data on the other large moons.' 'Juice and Europa Clipper are independent missions with individual science goals.'
evidence.supports: E2c: Juice and Europa Clipper are completely different, independent missions by different agencies.

evidence.snippet: 'Juice is a unique mission. It will be the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than our own... It will first orbit Jupiter, performing numerous flybys of the planet's moons – including 12 of Ganymede.' Entire article describes orbital observations and flybys only; no landing capability mentioned.
evidence.supports: E2b: Juice does not land on ice; it orbits and performs flybys. Ganymede is the primary target.

evidence.snippet: 'It will arrive at Jupiter in 2031 and spend 2.5 years orbiting Jupiter, often flying within 200 to 1,000 kilometers... of the icy moons.' Describes flybys and orbital study only.
evidence.supports: E2b: Juice uses flybys and orbit, not landing. E2a: targets include Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.
